Petunjuk Belajar Untuk Siswa

Unit Overview

Jembatan pemahaman: Unit ini mempelajari legenda sebagai teks naratif. Bahasa Indonesia dipakai sebagai pengantar agar arah belajar jelas, sedangkan contoh, teks, kosakata, grammar, latihan, dan performa tetap dominan dalam bahasa Inggris.
Catatan belajar: Instruksi pengantar menggunakan Bahasa Indonesia sebagai jembatan pemahaman. Namun, teks utama, kosakata, latihan, reading, listening, grammar, writing, speaking, dan asesmen tetap dominan menggunakan Bahasa Inggris agar kemampuan bahasa kamu berkembang.

Pada unit ini, kamu akan belajar tentang legend atau legenda, yaitu cerita rakyat masa lalu yang dipercaya oleh masyarakat setempat sebagai kisah yang benar-benar terjadi atau berhubungan dengan asal-usul tempat, benda, peristiwa, atau kepercayaan lokal.

Unit ini dekat dengan kehidupan siswa wilayah kepulauan atau pesisir: laut, pulau, dermaga, kapal, karang, sumur air tawar, musim barat, ombak besar, cerita orang tua, dan tradisi lisan masyarakat.

What You Will Learn

  1. memahami pengertian dan ciri-ciri legend;
  2. menganalisis struktur: orientation, complication, resolution, moral value;
  3. mengenali action verbs, simple past tense, past continuous tense, sequence words, direct speech, descriptive adjectives;
  4. membaca legenda lokal dalam bahasa Inggris;
  5. menyimak legenda dari daerah lain;
  6. menulis legenda pendek;
  7. menceritakan legenda melalui storytelling performance;
  8. merefleksikan nilai moral dan makna budaya.

Big Idea

Legends are not only old stories. They carry cultural memory, moral values, and the identity of a community.

Legends are often passed down from grandparents to parents, from parents to children, and from one generation to the next. In island communities, legends may be connected to the sea, reefs, stones, caves, wells, old boats, storms, or sacred places.

A legend may not be a scientific explanation, but it can teach people how to live wisely.

Essential Questions

  1. Why do people still tell legends today?
  2. What makes a story become a legend?
  3. Can a legend teach people how to behave?
  4. What local places in your island or coastal area have stories behind them?
  5. How can young people preserve local legends in English?
  6. What moral values are important in island communities?

Useful Expressions

  • “I think legends are important because…”
  • “In my community, people still talk about…”
  • “A legend usually teaches us to…”
  • “The moral value of the story is…”
  • “This story reminds people not to…”

ListeningStudents can understand spoken legends and arrange events chronologically.
GrammarStudents can use action verbs, past tense, sequence words, and direct speech in narrative texts.

B. Concept Exploration

What Is a Legend?

Penjelasan singkat: Legend bukan hanya cerita lama. Dalam pembelajaran English narrative, legend dipelajari sebagai teks yang memiliki tujuan sosial, struktur cerita, unsur bahasa, dan nilai moral. Fokusmu bukan menghafal definisi, tetapi memahami cara cerita dibangun dan cara menceritakannya kembali dalam English.

Petunjuk: Bagian ini menjelaskan konsep dasar legenda. Bacalah penjelasan dalam bahasa Inggris, lalu gunakan catatan Bahasa Indonesia sebagai jembatan pemahaman.

Definition of Legend

A legend is a traditional story from the past that is connected to a particular place, person, object, or event. A legend is often believed by a community as a story that may have really happened, although it may contain extraordinary or supernatural elements.

Dalam Bahasa Indonesia, legenda adalah cerita rakyat masa lalu yang dipercaya masyarakat setempat sebagai kisah yang berkaitan dengan asal-usul tempat, benda, kejadian, atau tokoh tertentu.

Examples of Legends

  • a story about why a lake was formed;
  • a story about a person who became stone;
  • a story about a sacred reef near an island;
  • a story about a mysterious cave;
  • a story about a well that appears only during certain seasons;
  • a story about a boat that never returned from the sea.

Social Function of Legend

  • entertain readers or listeners;
  • explain the origin of a place, object, or natural phenomenon;
  • teach moral values;
  • preserve cultural memory;
  • pass local wisdom from one generation to another;
  • warn people about wrong behavior;
  • strengthen community identity.

In island communities, legends often teach people to respect the sea, share water, keep promises, protect coral reefs, help neighbors, and listen to elders.

Characteristics of Legend

CharacteristicExplanationExample
Set in the pastThe story happened long ago.Long ago, there was a village near the shore.
Connected to a placeThe story explains a lake, stone, reef, cave, or island.The stone is believed to be a young man who broke his promise.
Human charactersThe main characters are often ordinary people.A fisherman, a mother, a child, a villager.
Extraordinary eventsSomething unusual happens.A person turns into stone.
Moral conflictA character faces a moral problem.Greed, arrogance, betrayal, disobedience.
Moral valueThe story teaches a lesson.Respect parents, keep promises, protect nature.
Oral traditionThe story is passed down orally.Grandparents tell the story to children.

Legend vs Other Story Types

Text TypeMain FocusCharactersSettingExampleKey Difference
LegendOrigin of place/object/local beliefHumans, villagers, ancestorsSpecific placeMalin Kundang, Lake TobaOften believed by local people
MythSacred belief, gods, creationGods, spirits, supernatural beingsAncient/cosmic worldCreation mythsMore connected to sacred belief
FolktaleEntertainment and wisdomOrdinary people, trickstersVillage/forest/kingdomTimun MasUsually not tied to real place
FableMoral lesson through animalsTalking animalsForest/farmThe Tortoise and the HareAnimals act like humans
Fairy TaleMagic and fantasyPrinces, princesses, witchesImaginary kingdomCinderellaUsually magical and fictional
Historical RecountFactual past eventReal historical peopleReal placesIndependence eventsBased on evidence/history

Narrative Structure of Legend

StructureFunctionGuiding Questions
OrientationIntroduces characters, setting, and situationWho? Where? When?
ComplicationShows the problem or conflictWhat went wrong?
ClimaxThe most intense part of the conflictWhat was the turning point?
ResolutionShows how the problem endsHow was the problem solved?
Reorientation/Moral ValueGives final message or lessonWhat can we learn?

D. Reading Section

Reading: The Legend of the Thousand Wells

Arah membaca: Bacalah teks pertama untuk menangkap gambaran umum, lalu baca ulang untuk menemukan orientation, complication, resolution, action verbs, past tense, sequence words, dan moral value. Jangan langsung menerjemahkan kata per kata.

Petunjuk: Kamu akan membaca legenda yang dibuat berdasarkan konteks kepulauan. Bacalah dulu tanpa kamus untuk memahami gambaran umum. Setelah itu, baca kembali untuk mencari struktur teks, kosakata penting, dan nilai moral.

Before Reading

  1. What happens when people on a small island do not have enough fresh water?
  2. Why should people share water fairly?
  3. What might happen if someone becomes greedy during a difficult season?
  4. Have you ever heard a local story about a well, a reef, a stone, or an island?

The Legend of the Thousand Wells

Long ago, there was a small island surrounded by blue water, white sand, and sharp coral reefs. The island was beautiful, but life there was not always easy. During the rainy season, the villagers collected water in jars, buckets, clay pots, and old bottles. During the dry season, however, the sun burned the ground, the leaves turned yellow, and fresh water became more precious than gold.

Most villagers were fishermen, seaweed farmers, boat makers, and small traders. Every morning, men sailed before sunrise, women prepared food and dried seaweed, and children helped their parents before going to school near the shore. They did not have many things, but they had one strong value: people must help one another to survive.

In the middle of the island, there was a wide sandy field. The elders said that under the white sand, fresh water sometimes appeared when the tide rose. During the dry season, the villagers dug small holes in the field. If they waited patiently, clear water slowly filled the bottom of the holes. The villagers called the place The Field of Little Wells.

There was one important rule. Every family could take only enough water for one day. Nobody was allowed to take more than they needed. The oldest woman in the village, Nenek Sari, always reminded the children, “Water is a gift. If you respect it, it will stay. If you are greedy, it will leave.”

Most villagers obeyed the rule. But one young man named Lampa did not.

Lampa was strong, handsome, and clever. He could sail farther than other young men, and he could dive longer than most fishermen. Unfortunately, he was also arrogant. He believed that rules were made for ordinary people, not for someone as strong as him.

One morning, after three months without rain, the villagers walked to the Field of Little Wells. Their jars were empty, and their faces looked tired. Nenek Sari stood near the biggest well and said, “Take only what you need. Remember, the wells belong to all of us.”

The villagers nodded. They filled their jars carefully. Some took water for cooking. Others took water for drinking. A mother gave her first cup of water to her sick child. Everyone moved slowly because they knew the water was limited.

Lampa arrived late, carrying two large containers. He looked at the small wells and laughed. “Why should I take only a little?” he said. “I am stronger than all of you. I can carry more, so I deserve more.”

Nenek Sari looked at him sadly. “Strength is not a reason to be greedy,” she said. “The sea gives fish to many boats, not only to one boat. The wells give water to many families, not only to one man.”

But Lampa ignored her. He filled one container, then another. When a little boy asked for space near the well, Lampa pushed him away.

“Wait for your turn,” Lampa said.

“This is my turn,” the boy answered quietly. “My grandmother is thirsty.”

The villagers became silent. Lampa looked at them and felt proud, not ashamed. He carried the two containers home and hid them under his house.

That afternoon, the wind stopped. The coconut leaves did not move. The sea became strangely flat, as if it were holding its breath. Then, from the center of the island, a low sound came from under the sand.

At first, the villagers thought it was thunder. But the sky was clear. Then they heard it again.

Dummm… dummm… dummm…

The ground trembled. The children ran to their parents. Nenek Sari closed her eyes and whispered, “The water is leaving.”

The villagers rushed to the Field of Little Wells. What they saw made them cry. The wells were dry. The white sand had cracked. Not even one drop of water remained.

Everyone was frightened. Some people prayed. Others looked at Lampa’s house. They knew what he had done, but no one spoke.

That night, Lampa could not sleep. He heard a soft voice from under his house.

“Return what you took.”

He sat up quickly. “Who is there?” he shouted.

The voice came again, softer but deeper.

“Return what you took.”

Lampa looked at the containers. They were still full of water. He wanted to return them, but his pride was stronger than his fear.

“No,” he whispered. “I carried the water myself. It is mine.”

Suddenly, the containers cracked. Water flowed out, but instead of wetting the ground, it turned into white sand. Lampa screamed and ran outside. The villagers came out of their houses and saw him standing under the moonlight.

Nenek Sari walked toward him. “Lampa,” she said, “you still have time. Ask for forgiveness. Take the sand back to the wells and promise to share.”

Lampa’s hands trembled. For the first time, he looked afraid. He knelt and said, “I was wrong. I thought strength meant taking more. I forgot that strength should protect others.”

The villagers did not cheer. They simply watched. Regret must be proven by action.

Before sunrise, Lampa carried the white sand back to the Field of Little Wells. He dug with his own hands. He dug one hole, then another, then another. The villagers saw him working, but nobody helped at first. They wanted to see if he was truly sorry.

By midday, his hands were wounded. Sweat fell from his face. He was tired and thirsty, but he did not stop. A little boy, the same boy he had pushed away, came near him and gave him a small cup of water.

Lampa looked at the boy in surprise. “Why do you help me?” he asked.

The boy answered, “Because my grandmother says water should not teach us to hate. It should teach us to live.”

Lampa cried. Then he continued digging.

When the sun almost disappeared behind the sea, Lampa had dug many small holes across the sandy field. Suddenly, the tide rose. The sound of waves came closer. The villagers waited quietly.

Then, slowly, water appeared at the bottom of one hole. A child shouted, “Water!”

Another hole filled with water. Then another. Then another. Soon, hundreds of little wells shone under the evening sky like small mirrors.

Nenek Sari smiled and said, “The water has returned, but it has also given us a lesson.”

From that day on, the villagers no longer called the place The Field of Little Wells. They called it The Thousand Wells. Lampa changed too. He became the first person to arrive at the wells every morning, not to take water first, but to make sure the old, the sick, and the children received water before him.

People say that until today, when the dry season comes and the tide rises, water still appears under the white sand. The elders tell the children, “Remember Lampa. Greed dries the heart, but sharing brings water back to life.”

And that is why the Thousand Wells are not only holes in the sand. They are a memory of a village that learned to survive together.

Reading Comprehension

Literal Questions

  1. Where did the story take place?
  2. What did the villagers collect during the rainy season?
  3. What happened during the dry season?
  4. What was The Field of Little Wells?
  5. What rule did the villagers have about water?
  6. Who was Nenek Sari?
  7. What kind of person was Lampa at the beginning?
  8. Why did Lampa take more water than others?
  9. What happened to the wells after Lampa’s action?
  10. How did Lampa prove his regret?

Inferential Questions

  1. Why was water described as “more precious than gold”?
  2. Why did Nenek Sari say, “Water is a gift”?
  3. What does the sentence “the sea became strangely flat, as if it were holding its breath” suggest?
  4. Why did the villagers not help Lampa at first?
  5. Why did the little boy give water to Lampa?
  6. What does Lampa’s change tell us about responsibility?
  7. Why did the water return after Lampa dug the wells?
  8. What does The Thousand Wells symbolize?

Analytical Questions

  1. How does the island setting influence the conflict?
  2. What values are important in the village community?
  3. How does Lampa change from the beginning to the end?
  4. What is the role of Nenek Sari in the story?
  5. Why is the little boy’s action important?
  6. How does the legend connect human behavior and nature?
  7. What makes this text a legend?
  8. What local issue in your area is connected to this story?

Evaluative Questions

  1. Do you think Lampa deserves forgiveness? Why?
  2. Was it fair that the villagers did not help Lampa at first?
  3. What would happen if Lampa never admitted his mistake?
  4. What moral value is most relevant for students today?
  5. Can this legend help people care more about natural resources?

Listening: The Legend of the Crying Stone

The Legend of the Crying Stone

Long ago, in a village near a hill, there lived a poor widow and her only daughter. The mother worked hard every day. She cooked, cleaned, carried firewood, and sold vegetables at the market. Her daughter, however, did not like helping her. The girl was very beautiful, but she was also proud and lazy.

Every morning, the mother asked her daughter to help with simple work. “Please help me carry these vegetables to the market,” said the mother.

The daughter usually answered, “I do not want to look poor. People will laugh at me.”

One day, the mother and daughter went to the marketplace together. The mother carried a heavy basket on her back, while the daughter walked in front of her wearing her best clothes. Many people looked at the girl and admired her beauty.

A young man asked, “Is the woman behind you your mother?”

The daughter felt ashamed. She did not want people to know that the poor woman was her mother. So she answered, “No, she is not my mother. She is only my servant.”

The mother heard the answer, but she stayed silent. Her heart was broken.

A few minutes later, another person asked the same question. Again, the daughter denied her mother. “She is just someone who follows me,” she said.

The mother could not hold her sadness anymore. She looked up to the sky and prayed, “If my daughter is truly ashamed of me, let her understand the pain of a mother’s heart.”

Suddenly, the sky became dark. The daughter felt her feet becoming heavy. She tried to walk, but she could not move. Slowly, her legs turned into stone.

“Mother! Help me!” she cried.

The mother ran to her, but it was too late. The girl’s body continued turning into stone. Tears fell from her eyes as she regretted her words.

Since then, people have called the stone “The Crying Stone.” The legend reminds children to respect their parents and never be ashamed of the people who love them.

F. Grammar Focus

Grammar for Writing and Telling Legends

Penjelasan grammar: Grammar di sini dipakai untuk membuat cerita lebih jelas. Simple past tense menunjukkan peristiwa masa lampau, action verbs membuat cerita hidup, sequence words mengatur alur, dan direct speech membuat konflik terasa nyata.

Petunjuk: Grammar pada unit ini tidak dipelajari sebagai rumus kosong. Kamu akan menggunakannya untuk membaca, menulis, dan menceritakan legenda.

1. Action Verbs

Action verbs show what characters do. In legends, action verbs make the story alive.

Weak sentence: The boy went to the cave.

Stronger sentence: The boy rushed into the forbidden cave.

Weak sentence: The woman said something.

Stronger sentence: The woman whispered a warning.

Practice 1: Improve the Verbs

Replace the weak verbs with stronger action verbs. Choose from: rushed, whispered, trembled, sailed, discovered, carried, escaped, protected, shouted, regretted

1. The fisherman went across the sea.
2. The girl said a secret.
3. The villagers were afraid.
4. The child found a hidden well.
5. The mother brought a jar of water.
6. The boy got away from the cave.
7. The reef kept the village safe.
8. The elder said loudly, “Stop!”
9. The young man felt sorry for his greed.
10. The villagers moved quickly to the shore.

2. Simple Past Tense

Legends mostly use simple past tense because they tell events from the past.

Positive

Subject + Verb 2 + Object/Complement

Lampa took more water than he needed.

Negative

Subject + did not + Verb 1 + Object/Complement

Lampa did not obey the rule.

Question

Did + Subject + Verb 1 + Object/Complement?

Did Lampa return the water?

Time Signals in Legends

long ago • once upon a time • in ancient times • one day • that night • the next morning • many years ago • from that day on • since then

4. The daughter ___ her mother in the marketplace.

3. Past Continuous Tense

Past continuous tense is used for an action that was happening at a certain time in the past.

Subject + was/were + Verb-ing
  • The villagers were waiting near the shore.
  • Lampa was carrying two containers.
  • The mother was praying when the sky became dark.
  • The children were playing when the ground trembled.

Use past continuous with simple past tense to show interruption.

The villagers were waiting near the wells when the ground trembled.
Practice 5: Combine the Sentences
  1. The villagers waited near the shore. The storm came.
  2. The mother prayed. The sky became dark.
  3. Lampa carried water. He heard a strange voice.
  4. The children played near the beach. The tide rose.
  5. The fishermen sailed home. A huge wave appeared.
  6. The daughter walked proudly. A young man asked about her mother.
  7. The elders talked near the well. The ground trembled.
  8. The boy dug the sand. Water appeared.

4. Sequence Words and Connectors

Sequence words help readers follow the plot.

Without sequence words

Lampa took the water. The wells became dry. He heard a voice. He returned the sand. The water came back.

With sequence words

First, Lampa took more water than he needed. Then, the wells became dry. That night, he heard a mysterious voice. After that, he returned the sand to the wells. Finally, the water came back.

Correct order: ___ - ___ - ___ - ___ - ___ - ___

5. Direct Speech

Direct speech makes a legend more dramatic and emotional.

Direct speech: “Water is a gift,” said Nenek Sari.
Indirect speech: Nenek Sari said that water was a gift.
Direct speech: “I will return before sunset,” said the fisherman.
Indirect speech: The fisherman said that he would return before sunset.
Practice 8: Identify Direct Speech
  1. “Do not enter the cave,” said the elder.
  2. The boy promised to return before sunset.
  3. “The sea is angry tonight,” whispered the grandmother.
  4. The villagers believed that the stone was sacred.
  5. “I am sorry,” said Lampa.
Practice 9: Change into Indirect Speech
  1. “I am not afraid,” said Lampa.
  2. “The wells belong to everyone,” said Nenek Sari.
  3. “I will help my grandmother,” said the boy.
  4. “The sea is becoming dark,” said the fisherman.
  5. “You must keep your promise,” said the elder.
G. Writing Section

Write Your Own Island Legend

Jembatan menulis: Menulis legend tidak dimulai dari kalimat panjang. Mulailah dari ide tempat, tokoh, konflik, perubahan tokoh, dan nilai moral. Setelah kerangka jelas, barulah kamu menyusun teks dalam English.

Petunjuk: Sekarang kamu akan menulis legenda. Jangan langsung menulis panjang. Ikuti tahapannya: pilih ide, rancang tokoh, tentukan konflik, susun alur, lalu tulis draf.

Writing Task: Write a legend about an island, reef, well, cave, stone, tree, boat, or other local place/object. Your legend should teach a moral value and show cultural meaning.

Basic target

350–450 words

Recommended target

500–700 words

Challenge

800 words or more

Choose Your Legend Idea

  1. A reef that whispers during the dry season
  2. A well that appears only when people share water fairly
  3. A stone that looks like a person waiting for a boat
  4. An island that disappears in the mist
  5. A cave that protects people from storms
  6. A tree that grows where someone kept a promise
  7. A boat that became stone after its owner became arrogant
  8. A shell that brings warnings from the sea
  9. A shore that teaches people to respect nature
  10. A local story from your family or community

Story Planning Template

Character Builder

A good character is not perfect. A character usually has strength and weakness.

Character ExampleStrengthWeaknessPossible Conflict
A young fishermanbravearrogantignores a storm warning
A seaweed farmerhardworkingimpatientbreaks a promise
A studentcuriouscarelessenters a forbidden cave
A traderclevergreedydestroys coral for money
A daughterbeautifulashameddenies her mother

Setting Builder

SenseGuiding QuestionsExample
SightWhat can people see?white sand, sharp coral, dark cave
SoundWhat can people hear?waves, wind, wooden boats
SmellWhat can people smell?salt water, dried fish, smoke
TouchWhat can people feel?hot sand, cold stone, rough coral
EmotionWhat is the atmosphere?mysterious, peaceful, tense

Conflict Ideas

  1. A character breaks a promise.
  2. A character becomes greedy.
  3. A character refuses to respect parents.
  4. A character destroys nature.
  5. A character lies to the community.
  6. A character ignores an elder’s warning.
  7. A character becomes arrogant after success.
  8. A character forgets to help others.
  9. A character uses power selfishly.
  10. A character learns courage through sacrifice.

Writing the Orientation

The orientation introduces the characters and setting.

Long ago, on a small island surrounded by coral reefs, there lived a young fisherman named Raka. He was brave and skillful, but he often ignored the advice of the village elders.

Writing the Complication

The complication shows the main problem.

One day, Raka entered the forbidden cave although the elders had warned him. Inside the cave, he found a shining shell and decided to take it home.

Writing the Resolution

The resolution shows how the problem is solved.

After the storm destroyed his boat, Raka returned the shell to the cave. He asked for forgiveness and promised to protect the shore.

Adding Moral Value

  • The story teaches us that…
  • From this legend, we learn that…
  • The moral value of the story is…
  • This legend reminds us to…
  • Since then, people have remembered that…
The story teaches us that nature should not be treated as personal property.
This legend reminds us to respect elders and keep our promises.
Model Text 1: Short Legend — The Legend of the Silent Shell

Long ago, there was a small island where people lived from the sea. Every fisherman carried a shell before sailing because they believed the shell could remind them to return safely.

A young fisherman named Rano was brave, but he was careless. One day, he laughed at the elders and threw his shell into the sea. “I do not need old beliefs,” he said.

Suddenly, the wind stopped. The waves became silent. Rano’s boat did not move although he pushed it with all his strength. Then he heard a soft voice from the water: “A person who forgets gratitude will lose direction.”

Rano became afraid. He took the shell from the water and held it carefully. “I am sorry,” he whispered.

After that, the wind returned and his boat moved again. Since then, fishermen on the island have kept shells in their boats, not because they fear the sea, but because they remember to be grateful.

Moral value: We should respect tradition and be grateful for protection.

Model Text 2: Medium Legend with Annotations — The Legend of the Stone Boat

Long ago, near a narrow strait between two islands, there lived a young boat maker named Sakka. He was famous because his boats were strong and fast. Many fishermen trusted his work.

However, Sakka became arrogant. He began to use weak wood for poor villagers and strong wood only for rich buyers. His father warned him, “A boat carries life, not only money.” But Sakka ignored him.

One day, a poor widow asked Sakka to repair her small boat. She needed the boat to visit her sick son on another island. Sakka took her money but repaired the boat carelessly.

That evening, the widow sailed across the strait. Suddenly, strong wind came. The boat cracked in the middle of the sea. The villagers rushed to help her, and luckily she survived.

When Sakka heard the news, he was ashamed. But before he could speak, the half-broken boat floated back to the shore by itself. Under the moonlight, the boat slowly turned into stone.

Sakka knelt beside it and cried. He promised to repair every boat honestly. From that day on, people called the place The Stone Boat Shore. Parents told their children, “Work is not only about profit. Work is also about responsibility.”

PartExplanation
OrientationIntroduces Sakka, the setting, and his skill.
ComplicationSakka becomes arrogant and repairs the widow’s boat carelessly.
ClimaxThe widow almost dies in the broken boat.
ResolutionThe boat turns into stone and Sakka learns responsibility.
Moral ValueWork must be done honestly and responsibly.

Storytelling Performance

Petunjuk: Storytelling bukan hanya membaca teks. Kamu harus membuat pendengar merasa masuk ke dalam cerita melalui suara, ekspresi, jeda, dan gerakan tubuh.

What Makes Good Storytelling?

Voice Control

ElementMeaningPractice

Pacespeed of speakingSlow down during important parts.
Pauseshort stopPause before the climax.

Storytelling Opening

  1. “Good morning, everyone. Today, I would like to tell you a legend from a small island.”
  2. “Let me take you back to a time when people listened to the sea and respected every drop of water.”
  3. “This is a story about a young person who learned that strength means protecting others.”

Storytelling Closing

  1. “That is the end of the story. From this legend, we learn that greed can hurt a community.”
  2. “This legend reminds us to share, respect nature, and keep our promises.”
  3. “Since then, people have remembered that water is not only a resource, but also a responsibility.”

  2. Suddenly, the wind stopped and the sea became silent.
  3. The villagers rushed to the shore.
  4. The young fisherman broke his promise.
  5. From that day on, people remembered the legend.

Speaking Activities

Activity 1: Pair Retelling

Student A tells the orientation. Student B continues the complication. Student A ends with the resolution.

Activity 2: 60-Second Story Challenge

Tell a legend in only 60 seconds. Include character, setting, problem, ending, and moral value.

Activity 3: Emotion Reading

Read “You still have time to return what you took.” as angry, sad, mysterious, gentle, and frightened.

Activity 4: Group Storytelling Circle

Each student continues one sentence. Example: “Long ago, there was a small island…”

K. Mini Project

Preserving Our Island Legend

Petunjuk: Kamu akan membuat proyek kecil untuk melestarikan cerita lokal atau legenda yang terinspirasi dari kehidupan kepulauan.

Project Goal: You will preserve a local or island-inspired legend by writing it in English and performing it through storytelling.

Choose One Project Type

  1. Write a new legend inspired by island life.
  2. Retell a local story from your family or community in English.
  3. Interview an older person about a local story, then write an English version.
  4. Create a storytelling performance based on your written legend.

Project Steps

  1. Choose your legend idea.
  2. Ask permission if the story comes from family or community oral tradition.
  3. Write notes about setting, characters, conflict, and moral value.
  4. Draft your legend in English.
  5. Revise grammar, vocabulary, and structure.
  6. Practice storytelling.
  7. Perform in front of the class or record your performance.
  8. Reflect on what you learned.
Ethical Note: Respect local culture. Do not mock local beliefs. If a story includes supernatural elements, present them as folklore, traditional belief, or local legend. Do not present them as scientific facts. Focus on moral values and cultural meaning.

Final Product

  • written legend: 500–800 words;
  • story map;
  • vocabulary list: minimum 20 words;
  • moral value paragraph;
  • storytelling performance: 3–5 minutes;
  • reflection paragraph.

M. Summative Assessment

Multiple Choice Questions A–E

Cara mengerjakan: Soal LOTS meminta informasi langsung dari teks. Soal MOTS meminta pemahaman struktur, makna, dan hubungan antarbagian cerita. Soal HOTS meminta kamu menilai moral value, simbol, relevansi dengan kehidupan siswa, atau kemungkinan adaptasi modern.

Petunjuk: Kerjakan soal berikut dengan teliti. Soal disusun dari level LOTS, MOTS, dan HOTS. Bacalah teks dengan saksama sebelum memilih jawaban.

Text 1 for Questions 1–10: The Legend of the Waiting Stone

Long ago, on a small island between two dangerous currents, there lived a girl named Maira. Her father was a fisherman who often sailed to other islands to sell dried fish. Before every journey, he always said, “Wait for me near the old tamarind tree. I will return before the full moon.”

One season, the waves became higher than usual. The villagers warned Maira’s father not to sail, but he needed money to buy medicine for Maira’s sick mother. He promised to return quickly and left before sunrise.

Every evening, Maira waited near the old tree. The first night passed. The second night passed. On the third night, the full moon appeared, but her father’s boat did not return. Some villagers told Maira to go home, but she refused.

Years passed. Maira still waited at the same place. Her hair became long, her clothes became pale, and her voice became soft like the wind. One morning, the villagers found a stone under the old tamarind tree. The stone looked like a girl sitting and facing the sea.

Since then, people have called it The Waiting Stone. Parents tell their children that love is powerful, but life must continue even when we lose someone.

Text 2 for Questions 11–20: The Reef That Cried

In a coastal village, there was a colorful reef where fish lived safely. The elders told the children, “Do not destroy the reef. It protects the shore and feeds the sea.”

A young trader named Balo did not care about the warning. He saw the reef only as a way to make money. One night, he secretly broke pieces of coral and loaded them onto his boat. His younger sister, Nira, saw him and begged, “Please stop. The reef is alive with stories.”

Balo laughed. “Stories cannot buy rice,” he said.

The next morning, fishermen found no fish near the village. The water looked grey. At night, people heard a crying sound from the sea. Nira went to the shore and returned the broken coral pieces. She apologized although she was not the one who had destroyed them.

Suddenly, the crying stopped. Small fish slowly returned to the reef. Balo watched silently. For the first time, he understood that the reef was not only stone; it was home.

Text 3 for Questions 21–30: The Cave of Returned Voices

Long ago, there was a cave on a quiet island. People believed that the cave returned every word spoken inside it. If someone spoke kindly, the cave returned a soft and beautiful echo. If someone spoke cruelly, the cave returned the words louder and sharper.

A student named Jali was known for his clever speech. He could make people laugh, but sometimes he used his words to embarrass others. His grandmother often said, “Words are like boats. Once they leave the shore, you cannot easily call them back.”

One afternoon, Jali entered the cave with his friends. To impress them, he shouted unkind words about an old fisherman who had recently lost his boat. His friends laughed for a moment. Then the cave returned his words again and again, louder each time.

The laughter stopped.

That evening, the old fisherman heard the echo from outside the cave. He said nothing, but his face looked deeply hurt. Jali wanted to apologize, but he felt too ashamed.

At night, Jali dreamed that he was trapped inside the cave. Every unkind word he had ever spoken flew around him like sharp stones. When he woke up, he ran to the fisherman’s house and apologized sincerely.

The next day, Jali returned to the cave. This time, he said, “May our words heal, not hurt.” The cave returned his sentence softly. Since then, children on the island have been taught to speak carefully, because every word may return to the speaker.

Short Answer Questions

Answer in 3–5 sentences.

  1. Explain why The Legend of the Thousand Wells can be called a legend.
  2. What moral value can students learn from Lampa?
  3. Compare Lampa from The Legend of the Thousand Wells and Balo from The Reef That Cried.
  4. Why are sequence words important in writing a legend?
  5. How can storytelling help preserve local culture?

Analytical Essay Questions

  1. Legends often connect human behavior with natural places. Explain how this connection appears in The Legend of the Thousand Wells or The Reef That Cried.
  2. Choose one character from the texts. Analyze how the character changes from the beginning to the end of the story.
  3. In your opinion, why should students in island communities learn to write local legends in English?

Then, he heard a voice calling his name. Suddenly, the wind pushed his boat toward the reef. After that, he promised to respect the cave. Finally, the villagers remembered the story as a warning.
